seo.title: Karmic tail 12 13 10 compatibility in a couple's matrix
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 13 10 compatibility: The Hanged Man, Death and The Wheel of Fortune — a language of waiting, the end of an old form and one shared wheel.

title: Karmic tail 12-13-10 in compatibility: the couple learning not to wait but to sail together
short: The karmic tail 12-13-10 in compatibility — The Hanged Man, Death and The Wheel of Fortune on the bottom line of the couple's matrix — poses a riddle: why does a couple whose shared language is loyalty and waiting have Death right in the middle? The short answer is this. The couple enters its task speaking a shared language of waiting: "let's wait", "later", "once I'm back, we'll start living". The middle of the road is Death: the end of that waiting and of the old shape of the union, not the end of love. The main task is the Wheel: to stop sitting out the turns apart, one on the road and the other on the shore, and to learn to go through them together, in their own rhythm of storms and quiet days.

sections.h2: Ceyx and Alcyone: the myth that holds the tail 12-13-10
paragraphs: In Book XI of the Metamorphoses (XI, 410–748; quoted here and below in the translation by Brookes More, 1922, where she is called Halcyone) Ovid tells of one of the most devoted married couples in ancient poetry. Ceyx is king of Trachis, a man "who had the fine countenance of Lucifer his father", the Morning Star. Alcyone is the daughter of Aeolus, master of the winds. Ceyx is troubled by ominous wonders and decides to sail to Apollo's oracle, "so sanctified to consolation of distress".

Alcyone turns pale. She is the daughter of the lord of the winds, and she argues from experience, not from fear: "for I knew them in my childhood and I often saw them from my father's home". If her husband cannot be held back, let him take her with him: "take me, too: some comfort may be gained, if in the storms we may be tossed together". Ceyx is moved — "the flame of love burned in his heart as strongly as in hers" — but he will neither cancel the voyage nor take her into danger. He makes a promise that calms her: he will come back "before the moon has rounded twice her orb".

Then come three acts. The ship sails; Alcyone watches her husband's face, then the ship, then the sail, until that too is gone. Halfway across, towards night, a storm wrecks the ship. Alcyone knows nothing: she counts the nights, gets clothes ready for his return and prays for a man who is no longer alive. Then Juno sends her a dream, and Morpheus, in the shape of the drowned Ceyx, tells her the truth. In the morning, on the shore, Alcyone sees a body in the waves, leaps from the mole — and rises as a bird. The gods change Ceyx too. The couple become kingfishers, and ever since, each winter, the sea has seven quiet days.
This is the tail 12-13-10 told as a story: waiting, the end of waiting, a shared wheel. What follows is the evidence, card by card.

sections.h2: The Hanged Man at the entry: a shared language of waiting
paragraphs: The entry to the task is the point where the couple makes its agreements. What it wants together, what words it uses for that, where it agrees without arguing. For Ceyx and Alcyone the shared agreement sounds like a deadline: "before the moon has rounded twice her orb…". Once it is said, things feel easier: "These promises gave hope of his return." An agreement about the future takes the anxiety out of the present. This is the language of The Hanged Man: life suspended until a date.

Then Ovid shows what such an agreement looks like from the inside. Alcyone "counts off the passing nights and hastens to prepare for him his clothes that he may wear as soon as he returns to her; and she is choosing what to wear herself, and vainly promises his safe return". She brings incense to Juno's shrine and prays "for Ceyx — after he had suffered death". Not a single bad deed, nothing but loyalty. And still it is a life in which the present has been pawned against the future.

In a modern couple this looks ordinary. One partner goes off into a long project, a rotation job, studies in another city: "six months, then it gets easier". The other keeps the home in "until they're back" mode: starts nothing new, plans no holiday, invites no guests, because "once they're back, we'll decide together". It can happen without anyone leaving at all: "we'll marry once we're on our feet", "we'll talk once things settle down", "we'll take care of ourselves once the children are older". Both wait honestly, and neither lives.

paragraphs.h3: The Hanged Man at its best: two people who sense each other at a distance

paragraphs: For Lisovskaya, The Hanged Man in a couple means tact, readiness to yield and a rare ability to sense each other at a distance. The myth takes this literally: on the night of the wreck Ceyx clings to a piece of the ship, "no other name is on his lips but hers", and "he is glad that she is safe at home". Before the ship has even left, Alcyone watches it "as if aware of future woe". Couples like this know something has happened to the other before a word is said; they call each other in the same minute; they can wait without reproach. It is a real gift.

paragraphs.h3: The Hanged Man at its worst: one person holds the relationship for both

paragraphs: The same gift turns into a weight. In the minus, Lisovskaya describes a couple in which one partner holds the relationship together with all their strength and gives up their own interests. Alcyone has one prayer the gods do grant — that her husband "might love her above all other women"; Ovid notes bitterly, "this one last prayer alone was granted to her". Loyalty is kept, but the waiting brings nothing back.

The entry to the task stands on the line of tasks, so the couple's wish can become its resistance. "Let's wait" starts to answer everything — even where there is nothing left to wait for. Waite insists that The Hanged Man is "life in suspension, but life and not death". Only a life put off until later one day demands to be lived now. That is why Death comes next in the tail.

sections.h2: Death in the middle: "Give up all deluding hopes of my return"
paragraphs: The middle of the task is what the couple goes through on the way from a shared wish to the main lesson. In Ovid this passage begins with a goddess who can no longer listen to prayers: "Juno could not long accept as hers these supplications on behalf of one then dead". Waiting stops being loyalty the moment one waits for what is no longer there.

A caveat first, without which this myth must not be laid over real people. In the Metamorphoses a man dies. In a couple's tail Death means neither dying nor breaking up: what dies is a form. The "until they're back" mode, the roles of "the one who left" and "the one who waits", the familiar image of the partner — all of this can end while the union stays. The card speaks of the end of a stage, not of what happens to people.

The truth reaches Alcyone from the house of Sleep, and Ovid describes it as a place outside time. There "the Sun, when rising or in middle skies, or setting, never can approach with light"; there "no wakeful bird with visage crested high calls forth the morning's beauty"; and "silent Rest is there". There is not even a door in this house: "No door is in that cavern-home and not a hinge's noise… disturbs the calm." Nothing rises, nothing sets, nothing turns. It is a house without a wheel.

In Hesiod's Theogony, Sleep and Death are children of Night and live side by side. The Hanged Man easily mistakes sleep for peace: "it'll sort itself out", "let's not touch it", "later". But in Hesiod sleep is Death's brother, not its substitute. And Juno takes her messenger precisely from the place where everything stands still — so that the sleep ends with the truth.

paragraphs.h3: "So do you come to me again?"

paragraphs: Morpheus stands by the bed in Ceyx's shape and says three things that couples do not say right away. The first: "can you still recognize your own loved Ceyx, or have my looks changed: so much with death you can not? — Look at me, and you will be assured I am your own". The second: "Give up all deluding hopes of my return." The third, that this is not hearsay: "it is no uncertain messenger that tells you this". The end of the old form has to be admitted plainly, not picked up from hints. Even in the dream Alcyone notices it: Brookes More has "he did not have his well known features", and Ovid's Latin adds that his face no longer shone as it used to — the face that once had "the fine countenance of Lucifer his father".

In the morning Alcyone goes down to the shore, to the spot where she saw her husband off. Something is floating in the waves. At first she weeps over a stranger: "Ah wretched one, whoever it may be, ah, wretched is the wife whom you have left!" Then she recognizes him: "It is he." And she speaks the key line of the middle: "So dearest one! So do you come to me again?" The promise to come back is kept — only not in the form anyone was waiting for.

In a couple this is a familiar scene. One partner returns from a long separation, a hard year, a move, the birth of a child, a new job — and returns changed. The other was waiting for the old one. "You've changed", "you used to be different" — that is Alcyone, seeing a stranger in her own person. Among the tasks of Death, Lisovskaya lists separations and long-distance relationships, and also a partner completely unlike the previous one, and the refusal to accept that difference. She means a previous partner; in the tail 12-13-10 the "previous one" is often the same person before the change. At its best the same energy gives a rare ability to accept change in a partner and move on. Wen calls the Death card "a call to let go of the present and move on", and for the reversed card she advises getting through it by being "fluid like water".

If the middle were counted from the ends, as in a personal matrix, it would be 12 + 10 = 22 — The Fool, a leap into the unknown. In the couple's tail Death stands in that place. But Ovid still has the leap, and it happens inside Death, not instead of it. Alcyone leaps onto the mole — "it seemed impossible" — and flies. Wen compares the suspension of The Hanged Man to the question The Fool presents: "will the Seeker fall or fly?" Here the answer is given: she flew — already in another shape.

Then Ovid leaves a question that fits any couple in the middle of this tail. Did Ceyx feel her touch, or did a wave simply lift his face? "All those who saw it doubted whether Ceyx could feel her kisses… But he was truly conscious of her grief." Change starts with one partner, and the other responds later, and not in a way everyone can see. But in the end both are transformed: a couple goes through the Death of this tail together, even if they do not start at the same time.

sections.h2: The Wheel of Fortune as the main task: "if in the storms we may be tossed together"
paragraphs: Lisovskaya reads the main task of a couple's tail mostly through the minus — it is what the couple cannot yet do. Her key to the Wheel is cyclicity: rises and crises take turns, and it is the turning itself that has to be accepted, not fought. In the minus there are swings between "silence" and "conflict", a habit of blaming fate and each other, a feeling that it is hard together but something holds them. Among the tasks of the Wheel are reaching a shared stability and overcoming fears together.

Now it is clear what went wrong in the myth from the very start. Alcyone fears the sea, and Ceyx sails into that sea alone. Each was left with their own share of fear: she on the shore, he on the waves. Her plea — "take me, too: some comfort may be gained, if in the storms we may be tossed together… together we can certainly endure" — is the formula of the main task. Not to avoid the storm, but to meet it as one fate for two.

In her despair Alcyone puts it even more precisely: had she gone with him, "I should have shared the whole course of my life with you and you would not have met a separate death." The couple's trouble is not the storm. The trouble is that for a while their fates became separate.

paragraphs.h3: Seven quiet days at the solstice

paragraphs: The ending of the myth answers her plea. After the change the two are "together in their fate" — in Latin fatis obnoxius isdem, "subject to the same fates". Now the couple has one fate. And Ovid ends: "Each winter during seven full days of calm Halcyone broods on her floating nest — her nest that sails upon a halcyon sea: the passage of the deep is free from storms, throughout those seven full days; and Aeolus restraining harmful winds, within their cave, for his descendants' sake gives halcyon seas."

These are the halcyon days — the source of the English phrase. Aristotle, in the History of Animals, says that "the name of 'halcyon days' is given to the seven days preceding, and to as many following, the solstice" — the winter solstice. The solstice is exactly the point where the wheel of the year turns; the word itself, Latin solstitium, says that the sun stands still at that moment. The calm comes not in spite of the turn but at its very point.

There is a detail no translation could keep. Brookes More has a "floating nest", but in the Latin the nests are pendentibus — hanging, from the same verb pendere that gives the Marseille card XII its French name, LE PENDU. The tail's Hanged Man comes back in the final picture of the myth. But now it hangs not outside the wheel, sitting it out, but inside it: seven days of rest that return every winter. At the start of the voyage the captain has the oars drawn up — Ovid's Latin calls them pendentes remos, hanging oars: from then on the wind carries the ship. At the end it is a nest that hangs, and the winds are held back for its sake.

Wen writes that the wheel on the card is "reminiscent of the mathematical concept of the unit circle", which can be expressed with sine and cosine, "revealing the philosophy of oscillations between zeniths and nadirs, highs and lows". A point on the rim of a turning wheel, if one follows only its height, draws a sine curve — a wave. Ovid paints the storm exactly like that: the ship "aloft as from a mountain peak it seemed to look down on the valley and the depth of Acheron", and then, "when sunk down in a trough of waves engulfing, it appeared to look up at the zenith from infernal seas".

And one coincidence that should be called a coincidence. In the Latin, Ceyx's ship is finished off by the tenth wave — decimae undae; Brookes More keeps it: "the tenth wave with known power, rushes more furious than the nine before". The Russian translator, Sergei Shervinsky, swapped it for the "ninth wave", the proverbial biggest wave of Russian speech. In the couple's tail the main task stands at number 10.

What this means for a couple whose main task is the Wheel. Not even Aeolus can cancel the storms: he keeps the winds locked up only seven days a year. The task is different — to know one's own rhythm. What do we do in a storm — and do we do it together. When are our quiet days — and do we protect them. Not to blame each other for the weather: a storm belongs to the sea, it is not the fault of the one who went to sea.

sections.h2: Waite's cards: a ship on Death and a serpent on the Wheel
paragraphs: The myth of Ceyx and Alcyone is not in Waite. But in his book and on the classic Waite–Pamela Colman Smith cards, each of the three cards of the tail has one detail that fits this story. These are coincidences, and they should be called coincidences — but there are three of them.

The Hanged Man. Waite ends his description of the card by promising that whoever understands its symbol "will know that after the sacred Mystery of Death there is a glorious Mystery of Resurrection". He starts speaking of Death already in the text on The Hanged Man. So does Wen: one of her readings of The Hanged Man is "the unsettling calm before a storm, before the difficult and painful transitions indicated in Key 13: Death". Both books read the first two cards of the tail as one sequence.

Death. Describing the picture, Wen notices a detail that is easy to miss: "A single ship sails on the river. Is it the River Styx?" On the horizon, between two pillars, a sun is rising — for Waite, "the sun of immortality". The ship leaves by water, the sun rises over water: one picture holds both the farewell and the morning after the night.

The Wheel of Fortune. Waite writes that the wheel stands "for the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe and for the flux of human life", and admits: "I have, however, presented Typhon in his serpent form" — the serpent glides down the descending side of the wheel, while Hermanubis rises on the other. In Hesiod, Typhon is the source of the wild winds that fall on the sea: "some rush upon the misty sea and work great havoc among men with their evil, raging blasts… scattering ships and destroying sailors". The storm that wrecked Ceyx's ship is drawn on the Wheel. But it is drawn on only one side of it.
The cards on the site are the site's own drawings, in places unlike the Waite deck; everything said here refers to the classic deck.

sections.h2: Strength at the centre: the mole that breaks the first wave
paragraphs: Every couple with the tail 12-13-10 has 11, Strength, at the centre of the couple's matrix. For Lisovskaya the centre is the shared atmosphere between the partners, what is inside the couple and not on show. Strength at its best means sensing finely what the other needs, energizing and strengthening each other, finding compromise without losing oneself. At its worst, a fight for leadership and "each has their own truth".

Waite connects Strength "with the Divine Mystery of Union" and reads its symbolism in Gospel words — "the sweet yoke and the light burden". The word "yoke" is no accident here. The Russian word for spouse, suprug, goes back, according to Vasmer's dictionary, to Old Russian suprug, "a pair in harness"; Latin coniunx, the word Ovid uses again and again for Ceyx and Alcyone, comes from the same image of a shared yoke, and English "conjugal" still carries it. Spouses are those who pull in one harness.

Ovid has an exact image for this strength. By the sea where Alcyone waited for her husband stands "a mole, made by the craft of man", which "adjoins the sea and breaks the shoreward rush of waves". A mole does not stop the sea — it takes the first blow. And it is from the mole that Alcyone takes flight. The atmosphere of Strength in such a couple is this mole: not a ban on storms but the shared skill of breaking the first, fiercest wave of a quarrel or a misfortune. At its worst the mole turns into a wall that each builds against the other.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or The Devil
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, its shared path. Couples with this tail have one of two numbers here: 6, The Lovers, in 57.2% of cases, or 15, The Devil, in 42.8%. And the myth of Ceyx and Alcyone has two ancient versions with opposite morals.

Ovid's version is about love that survived a change of form: an old man watches the kingfishers fly together across the sea and praises "their love, undying to the end". This is The Lovers: Waite calls it "in all simplicity the card of human love" and writes that it "replaces… the old card of marriage". The couple's value is a choice it makes again in every new shape.

Apollodorus's version, in the Library (I, 7, 4), is harsher: Ceyx and Alcyone "perished by reason of their pride; for he said that his wife was Hera, and she said that her husband was Zeus", and Zeus turned them into birds. This is already The Devil: a union in which two people become gods to each other and the whole world shrinks to the couple. A shadow of this version is in Ovid too — in Alcyone's cry: "Alas, Halcyone is no more! no more! with her own Ceyx she is dead! is dead!" Without the other, there is no self. Waite writes of The Devil: "Hereof is the chain and fatality of the material life." Lisovskaya's closing thought on The Devil in a couple is that no one belongs to anyone.
Both versions end with the same birds. The difference is in how the couple explains its shared fate: by choice — or by a chain.

sections.h2: How the tail 12-13-10 is formed: the calculation and the evidence in the numbers
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The middle of the couple's tail is not recalculated from its ends: it is added up from the partners' personal middles. An example — the dates 05.12.1975 and 06.03.1978.

The partners' personal tails are 18-3-12 and 21-10-16, their centres 6 and 5, and the couple's centre is 6 + 5 = 11, Strength. The couple's values for these dates are 15, The Devil. If the ends of the couple's tail were added together as in a personal matrix, the result would be 12 + 10 = 22, The Fool, not 13.
The evidence in the numbers — checked by running every date through the site's engine:

ul: **Rarity.** The tail 12-13-10 occurs in about one couple in 401 — 0.249%, 69th place out of 97 couple tails. There are no other couple tails made of the same three numbers: the order 12-13-10 is the only one.

**No person has this tail.** In a personal matrix the entry M equals the main task D plus the centre. For the entry to be 12 when D = 10, the centre would have to be 2, and no person has such a centre. This story is born only between two people.
**Three roads to one tail.** The tail comes from three combinations of personal tails: 18-3-12 + 21-10-16 in 50% of such couples, 6-5-17 + 6-8-20 in 35%, 18-6-15 + 21-7-13 in 15%.

**A Death that belonged to no one.** In 85% of such couples there is no 13 in either personal tail: the couple's Death is made of The Empress and the Wheel (3 + 10), The Hierophant and Justice (5 + 8), or The Lovers and The Chariot (6 + 7). In her reading of one couple, Lisovskaya writes about 13 specifically: when the partners themselves do not have it, the couple lives it out together, and for both it is a new experience. Only in 15% of couples does one partner have Death — as their personal main task; in the couple's tail it moves to the middle.

**The pause and the turn come from different houses.** In half of the couples both end cards of the couple's tail are already present in the partners, but separately: one has The Hanged Man as their personal main task, the other has the Wheel in their personal middle. The couple gathers into one story what each had on their own. In 35% of couples both partners enter their personal tails with The Lovers, and 6 + 6 give The Hanged Man.
**One centre for all.** Strength at the centre — in 100% of couples with this tail.

sections.h2: How a couple with the tail 12-13-10 can step out of waiting
paragraphs: A couple's tail is a task, not a verdict. The method gives no compatibility percentages and predicts no events: it shows where the same story keeps repeating in a couple. Here is what changes that story.

ol: **Wait with a deadline and a plan for "it didn't come".** The promise "before the moon has rounded twice her orb" calmed Alcyone, but it had no second half. The Hanged Man's agreement is more honest when it has a review date: how long we wait, and what we do if there is nothing left to wait for.

**Go through at least part of the hard road together.** "Take me, too" is not a whim but the main task of the Wheel. Travel as two, sit side by side in a hard conversation, share the risk instead of protecting each other by separation.
**Name the end of a form out loud.** Not a reproachful "you've changed" but "the way it was is over — who will we be now?". Morpheus speaks plainly, and only after plain words does the change begin.
**Don't live in the house of Sleep.** Silence, "it'll sort itself out" and "let's not touch it" look like peace, but in that house nothing turns. Rest without change is sleep, not peace.

**Find your own halcyon days.** A recurring stretch of calm that the couple shields from the winds: an evening, a weekend, a week a year. Not "once everything is fine" but by the calendar, as Aeolus does it.
**Don't close in on each other.** Lisovskaya advises a couple with the Wheel to have shared friends and new pursuits. A union where "there is no me without you" slides from The Lovers into The Devil.

paragraphs: The strong version of the tail 12-13-10 is a couple that can wait but does not hide in waiting; that can bury worn-out forms without burying each other; and that knows there are seven quiet days after the winter storms, because it has seen them more than once.

ul: **12, The Hanged Man — entry to the task.** What the couple wants together and the language in which it makes its agreements: stop the clock, wait it out, put life on hold "until". At its best this is loyalty and the gift of sensing each other at a distance; at its worst it is life suspended, where both wait honestly and neither lives.

**13, Death — middle of the task.** What the couple goes through: the old shape of the union comes to an end, and one partner comes back to the other changed. What dies is the waiting mode — not the people and not the relationship.

**10, The Wheel of Fortune — main task.** What the couple has to learn: rises and falls will keep taking turns, and arguing with the turning itself is useless. The task is one fate for two and quiet days of their own inside the circle.

intro: The solution is written in the cards and the numbers themselves. And two thousand years ago Ovid told it — in a myth where the three cards come in exactly this order.

faq.q: Is the tail 12-13-10 a bad sign for compatibility?
faq.a: No. For Lisovskaya a couple's tail is a karmic programme — tasks that show up mostly through the minus but can also sound in the plus. The method gives no compatibility percentages, and one line of the matrix does not decide the fate of a union. The tail 12-13-10 shows what the couple has to learn: to go through change together rather than wait it out apart.

faq.q: Does Death in a couple's tail mean a break-up?
faq.a: No. In the middle of the tail Death is the end of a form, not of people and not of the relationship: the waiting mode ends, the familiar roles end, the old image of the partner ends. In Ovid the union does not fall apart — both are transformed, and their love lives on. The card predicts neither losses nor dates.

faq.q: Why does neither partner have the tail 12-13-10?
faq.a: Because no personal matrix has this tail: with a main task of 10, an entry of 12 would need a centre of 2, and no person has one. A couple's tail is added up point by point from two personal tails — most often 18-3-12 and 21-10-16. And the Death in the middle, for most such couples, belongs to neither partner: it appears only in the couple.

report: Alcyone counts the nights until her husband's return and gets his clothes ready for when he comes home. By then Ceyx's ship is already wrecked, and she keeps going to the altar to pray "for Ceyx — after he had suffered death". This is how a story begins in Ovid's Metamorphoses (translated by Brookes More) in which the three cards of this tail come in exactly the order they hold in the couple: waiting, the end of waiting, a shared wheel.

The Hanged Man at the entry is the couple's shared language: stop the clock, wait it out, put life on hold "until". Death in the middle is what the couple goes through: what ends is not love and not the people, but the old shape of the union. The Wheel of Fortune as the main task is the lesson: to stop sitting out the turns apart and to learn to go through them together.

report.h3: An agreement that puts life on hold

report: Ceyx sails for an oracle; Alcyone begs him not to go, or, if he must, to take her with him. He does not take her, and promises to come back "before the moon has rounded twice her orb". After those words she feels easier: an agreement about the future takes the anxiety out of the present. **This is the language of The Hanged Man: life suspended until a date.**

At its best this is a rare gift. report: The turn begins with a goddess: Juno can no longer listen to prayers for a dead man and sends Alcyone a dream. The messenger is taken from the house of Sleep, where the sun neither rises nor sets and there is not even a door, so that "not a hinge's noise" breaks the calm. Nothing turns — a house without a wheel. That is the temptation of this tail: "it'll sort itself out", "let's not touch it", "later".

Morpheus, in the shape of the drowned Ceyx, speaks plainly: he asks whether death has changed his looks too much to be recognized — and then says the main thing: "Give up all deluding hopes of my return." **In a couple's tail Death means the end of a form, not dying and not a break-up.** What dies is the "until they're back" mode, the roles of "the one who left" and "the one who waits", the familiar image of the partner.

report.h3: Seven quiet days inside the wheel

report: Now it is clear where the story cracked from the very start. Alcyone fears the sea, and Ceyx sails into that sea alone; each is left with their own share of fear. Her plea on the shore — **"if in the storms we may be tossed together"** — is the formula of the main task. The trouble is not the storm but the fact that for a while their fates became separate.

The ending answers that plea. After the change the two are "together in their fate": now they have one fate. And each winter, "during seven full days of calm", Alcyone broods on her nest above the sea while Aeolus keeps the winds locked up. Aristotle places these halcyon days at the winter solstice — exactly the point where the wheel of the year turns. The calm comes not in spite of the turn but at its very point.

In the Latin the nests are pendentibus — hanging, from the same verb that gives the Marseille card XII its French name, LE PENDU. **The Hanged Man comes back in the ending, but now it hangs not outside the wheel, sitting it out, but inside it: seven days of rest that return every winter.** Not even Aeolus can cancel the storms. The couple's task is to know its own rhythm: what it does in a storm and whether it does it together, when its quiet days are and whether it protects them.

report.h3: Waiting with a deadline, not instead of living

report: The story changes not through sacrifice but through a few simple decisions:

ul: wait with a review date: for how long, and what to do if there is nothing left to wait for;
go through at least part of the hard road as two, instead of leaving one on the shore;
name the end of a form out loud: not a reproach that the other has changed, but "the way it was is over — who will we be now?";
not mistake silence and "it'll sort itself out" for peace;
set the quiet days by the calendar, as Aeolus does, rather than "once everything is fine".

report: The strong version of the tail 12-13-10 is a couple that can wait but does not hide in waiting; that buries worn-out forms without burying each other; and that knows there are seven quiet days after the winter storms, because it has seen them more than once.

unit.title: Seven calm days inside the wheel

captions.M: To agree to wait and put life on hold “until”
captions.N: To let the old shape go and know each other anew
captions.D: To go through the turns together and guard quiet days

unit.meaning: Your task is to stop sitting out the turns apart: go through them together and guard your quiet days.
